Discharge Summary:
Patient: 45-year-old female
Diagnosis: Multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer that affects the bone marrow

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with multiple purple and dark bruise-like patches on the skin. These patches appeared around the eyes, cheeks, and the front and back of the neck. The areas normally covered by clothing were mostly clear. These skin problems started 2 years ago. Even small bumps or injuries caused these patches to appear. The skin was very easy to damage in most areas. The patient also had several bouts of loose stools and fever over the past 6 months. A physical exam showed the patient was slightly pale and had swelling in both feet. A small sample of skin was taken and tested. It showed a blister-like problem with an abnormal protein buildup called amyloid. Blood tests and a bone marrow test confirmed the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. X-rays and other images of the bones looked normal.

Treatment:
The patient was sent to the blood cancer specialists. Treatment with cancer-fighting drugs was started.

Prognosis:
How well the patient does will depend on how the cancer responds to treatment. It will also depend on how far the cancer has spread. The patient should stay in close contact with the blood cancer care team.

Follow-up:
The patient should see the blood cancer specialists on a regular basis. The patient should also take all medicines as directed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 61-year-old male with a history of controlled type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and past smoking. He came to the hospital with lower back pain and weight loss.

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted to Internal Medicine because of lower back pain and weight loss. A CT scan showed broken bones and a growth near the left side of the spine. Doctors thought it might be cancer. More imaging tests showed a growth near the right lung and another in the upper left lung. There were also small spots that could be from infection or swelling. Doctors took a sample from the growth and found pus. Tests showed it contained tuberculosis bacteria. The patient started treatment with four medicines to fight tuberculosis, called HRZE. The patient also saw specialists for physical medicine and bone care. He received physical therapy to help him recover. After 25 days, the patient left the hospital. He was sent to continue physical therapy and to visit a special clinic for tuberculosis care.

Follow-up: The patient finished two months of treatment with four medicines. He is now taking two medicines to fight tuberculosis, called HR. The growths outside the lungs have gone away completely. A new CT scan of the lower back showed the growth there has gotten smaller.

Diagnosis: Long-term infection with swelling caused by tuberculosis.

Condition at discharge: Stable.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Patient: 15-year-old girl
Diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI), a condition where the body makes too much insulin, causing low blood sugar
Treatment: Diazoxide, Octreotide, Lanreotide

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient with CHI came to the children's hospital unit for a planned stay. The goal was to find a different medicine because diazoxide was causing unwanted hair growth.
The care team slowly lowered and then stopped diazoxide for 72 hours to see what would happen. However, this caused repeated episodes of low blood sugar with symptoms.
Octreotide was then started as a shot under the skin four times a day. This medicine helps control blood sugar.
The patient responded well to this dose. She was able to go without food for 24 hours with no low blood sugar.
Lanreotide was then started as a shot under the skin, 30 mg once a month. This is a long-acting medicine similar to octreotide. Octreotide was slowly lowered and then stopped.
A device that checks blood sugar all the time showed good blood sugar control after starting lanreotide. There were no episodes of low blood sugar.
The patient started having repeated low blood sugar episodes with symptoms after starting fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was stopped and the low blood sugar episodes went away within a week.
Two weeks after stopping fluoxetine, the patient's sad mood slowly got better over time with the help of talk therapy.

Final Diagnosis:
Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)

Follow-up Plan:
No further specific follow-up needed at this time.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient who came to our department with swelling inside the mouth on the left side of the lower jaw for six months. The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The patient was asleep under general anesthesia during the procedure.

History of Present Illness: The patient came to our department with swelling and pain in the left lower jaw area for six months. The swelling grew quickly after the patient had back teeth removed on the lower left side. The patient did not have a fever or trouble swallowing.

Physical Examination: When looking at the outside of the face, the lower left side looked uneven compared to the right side. There were no swollen lymph nodes in the area. When looking inside the mouth, there was a growing mass that spread from front to back and side to side. It went from the area of the first small back tooth to the area behind the last molar. The mass measured about 6 by 4 centimeters. The skin covering the mass looked normal in color and feel.

Diagnostic Tests: A panoramic jaw x-ray showed a clear dark area going from the lower left first small back tooth to the area behind the last molar. CT scans, which are detailed pictures of the inside of the body, showed the growth was breaking down bone in the lower left jaw. This bone loss went from the small back teeth area into the back part of the jawbone. A small tissue sample was taken and looked at under a microscope. This test confirmed the growth was an aggressive central giant cell granuloma, which is a type of noncancerous but fast-growing jaw tumor.

Hospital Course: The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The surgery was done from both outside and inside the mouth to remove all of the growth. The patient went home without any problems.

Follow-up: At checkup visits over the next year, there were no signs that the growth came back. This was checked by looking in the mouth and taking x-rays. The area under the chin where tissue was taken healed well with very little scarring. The small scar is not in a part of the face that people easily see.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 4-month-old baby girl. She was brought to the hospital because she was not making eye contact. She was born 5 weeks early at 35 weeks of pregnancy. There were no known health problems in the family. The patient was found to have Leber congenital amaurosis, also called LCA. This is a rare eye condition that causes severe vision loss. The doctors found this because her eyes turned inward and moved back and forth on their own. A test that checks how the back of the eye responds to light showed no response in both eyes. The patient also had trouble focusing her eyes, which was treated. The doctors did several exams. They looked at the front and back of her eyes. They also checked her whole body for problems with her organs or body chemistry. These tests were normal except for the eye problems already mentioned.

The doctors did many tests to find the cause. They did genetic testing to look for changes in certain genes. These tests did not find any problems. A brain scan called an MRI was done. It showed extra fluid in the spaces around the front parts of the brain. It also showed that a thin wall in the middle of the brain was missing. This wall is called the septum pellucidum. No other brain problems were found. The main connection between the two sides of the brain looked normal. The protective covering around nerves in the brain was developing normally. Later brain scans still showed the missing wall in the middle of the brain. The extra fluid around the brain stayed the same and did not get worse. The doctors thought about a condition called septo-optic dysplasia. However, the eye nerves looked normal and the hormone gland at the base of the brain worked normally. This made the doctors unsure about that diagnosis.

Medical History:
The patient had no other health problems. Her only issues were the eye condition called LCA and the brain scan findings with extra fluid around the brain.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient is a 4-month-old baby girl who came to the hospital for poor eye contact. She was found to have LCA, a condition that causes severe vision loss. The doctors did genetic testing and brain scans. Later brain scans still showed the missing wall in the middle of the brain. The extra fluid around the brain stayed the same. By age 3, the patient showed some delays in learning and development. No other health problems were found during her time in the hospital.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 65-year-old female with a history of thyroid disease was admitted to the hospital. She had been feeling tired and sick to her stomach for one week. She had no history of mental health problems. Her blood tests showed low sodium levels. Her heart test showed some unusual patterns.

Course:
After admission, the patient became more alert at first. Four days later, she started seeing things that were not there. She also became very suspicious of others. She was confused and restless. Mental health doctors were called to help. They gave her a medicine called quetiapine to help calm her confusion. On the same day, she felt sick to her stomach again. She became pale and started sweating. Doctors thought her heart might be failing. They did an emergency heart procedure to check her blood vessels. They found she had a heart condition called broken heart syndrome. This is a type of heart problem often caused by stress. Doctors gave her a steroid medicine called hydrocortisone. Within 3 days, her sodium levels and confusion got much better. A heart imaging test was done 10 days after starting the steroid. It showed her heart was pumping much better than before.

Diagnosis:
Blood tests showed her body was not making enough of certain stress hormones. These hormones are called cortisol and ACTH. Her urine tests also showed low levels of cortisol. Doctors found the patient had a rare condition. Her body could not make enough ACTH hormone. A brain scan was done to check the gland that makes this hormone. The scan showed no growths or problems in that area.

Discharge:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. She was told to keep taking hydrocortisone by mouth. She was told to see her regular doctor for follow-up care. She was also told to see a hormone specialist to manage her ACTH hormone problem.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Name Redacted]
Age: 65 years old
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: Skin cancer (melanoma) found in the urethra (the tube that carries urine out of the body). Some cancer cells were left at the edges after the first surgery.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to our hospital after having trouble urinating for 6 months. The patient also had a small growth at the opening where urine comes out. A physical exam showed a small tan growth sticking out from the urine opening. It looked like a common harmless bump. There were no signs of swollen glands in the groin area. Doctors removed the growth, and the patient recovered well from this surgery. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed it was skin cancer (melanoma) in the urethra. Some cancer cells were still at the edges of what was removed. More tests showed a small amount of cancer was still in the last half centimeter of the urethra. The upper part of the urethra and the bladder were normal. Doctors then did a second surgery to remove the entire urethra but kept the bladder. They created a new opening in the belly for the patient to empty the bladder using a thin tube. This surgery removed enough tissue to get 2.5 centimeters of healthy tissue around the cancer. The patient handled the surgery well and had no problems afterward.

Outcome:
The final lab report showed a very small spot (3 millimeters) of remaining skin cancer. This time, no cancer cells were found at the edges. Now, one year after surgery, the patient shows no signs of cancer.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient will need long-term checkups with regular tests and scans to watch for any return of the cancer. The patient must use a thin tube to empty the bladder on a regular schedule. The patient can control when to empty the bladder. The patient should see a cancer doctor and a bladder doctor for ongoing care and checkups.

The patient was admitted after being diagnosed with a rare genetic brain disease called CADASIL. This disease affects blood vessels in the brain. The patient came in with a history of dizziness, severe headaches, numbness and tingling in the hands and feet, memory loss, tiredness, sleeping too much, anxiety, and depression. After being admitted, a brain scan was done. The scan showed more damage to the white matter in the brain, including areas on both sides of the brain.

Treatment:

The patient did not receive any treatment during the first visit. The symptoms went away after a few months. Later, the patient developed severe headaches that did not get better with usual headache medicines. No treatment was given at that time. A brain doctor first thought the patient had multiple sclerosis. The patient was sent to a special clinic. A new brain scan showed damage in specific areas on both sides of the brain. This led to a diagnosis of CADASIL.

Consultations:

The patient saw a brain specialist who focuses on the immune system. The diagnosis was changed based on the new brain scan results. A genetic test for the NOTCH3 gene came back positive, which confirmed the diagnosis.

Follow Up:

The patient was told to see a brain doctor for ongoing care of their CADASIL.

Discharge:

The patient left the hospital with a diagnosis of CADASIL. The patient was told to follow up with a brain doctor. There were no problems during the hospital stay.

The patient is a 50-year-old male farmer who was sent to our hospital for emergency care. The patient came in with stomach pain that came and went. Two days before, he had surgery at another hospital to fix a hole in his small intestine and treat an infection that had spread in his belly.

When the patient first went to the other hospital, his kidneys were not working well. He had low potassium levels in his blood. He also had bad belly pain and was making very little urine for 5 days. After surgery, the patient had swelling in his face and trouble breathing. He also had too much acid in his blood, low blood pressure, confusion, and fever. The patient was put on a breathing machine and given medicines to fight infection. These medicines included aztreonam and metronidazole given through a vein. Even with all this care, the patient got worse.

Blood tests showed the patient had a low red blood cell count with some oddly shaped cells. Other test results showed the following. The patient had too many white blood cells and not enough cells that help blood clot. Tests that show swelling in the body were high. Kidney function tests showed the kidneys were not working well. Salt and potassium levels in the blood were too high. Liver tests were also high. An imaging test of the belly showed mild kidney disease and a small fluid buildup near the spleen. It also showed swollen tubes in the liver. A urine test showed a small number of cells that fight infection. A test of fluid from the belly showed some cells that fight infection along with yeast and fungus. A blood test for germs came back clean after 24 hours.

A test of belly fluid found a fungus called Trichosporon beigelii. Based on these tests, the infection was treated using standard medical care. Even with treatment, the patient kept getting worse. He was then sent here for emergency care.

Given how sick the patient is, he will keep getting care to support his body. More treatment will be given as needed.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was found to have an infection caused by a fungus called Trichosporon beigelii. This was treated during his hospital stay.

Follow-up Care:

The patient will keep getting follow-up care to make sure he gets the treatment he needs. Instructions for follow-up care will be given at future visits.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 8-year-old girl, was admitted because of vision loss in the right eye for 5 years. She also had headache and vomiting for 6 months. During the exam, the right eye could not see any light at all. The left eye had normal vision. A brain scan showed a fluid-filled sac on the right side of the brain. It measured about 8 by 9 by 6.5 centimeters. A small round lump was seen on the inner side of this sac, near the brain's fluid spaces. Doctors first thought it might be a type of brain tumor. Blood tests later showed that the thyroid gland was not working well due to a problem with hormone signals from the brain.

Treatment:
The patient had surgery to open the skull on the right side of the head. The surgeon drained the fluid-filled sac and created an opening so fluid would not build up again. The fluid inside was yellow and looked like thick oil. It contained fatty crystals and small bits, mostly on the inner side. Lab tests of the tissue showed the sac was a harmless cyst that had become swollen and irritated. The cyst wall was lined with flat to layered skin-like cells. It also had swollen blood vessels and signs of long-term irritation, including certain white blood cells grouped together.

Outcomes:
After surgery, the patient recovered without any problems. The headache and vomiting went away completely. The patient continues to see the doctor regularly. A brain scan done 6 months after surgery showed the cyst has not come back.

The patient is a 43-year-old white male who was generally healthy before this illness. He was admitted to the hospital because of ongoing fever, belly pain, back chest pain, and ear pain. He was found to have an outer ear infection and sent home with amoxicillin-clavulanate and paracetamol, both taken by mouth. Blood tests at that time showed higher than normal levels of CRP, a marker of swelling in the body, and ALT, a liver enzyme.

After leaving the hospital, the patient came back with dark urine, pale stool, and yellow skin and eyes. Swollen lymph nodes were found on both sides of the neck. No other problems were found during the physical exam, chest X-ray, or belly ultrasound.

The patient's blood tests showed a rise in white blood cells, a mild rise in lipase, a digestive enzyme, and higher bilirubin levels. He was given two strong antibiotics called Piperacillin-Tazobactam and Tigecycline. However, his condition got worse. Several of his organs began to fail, and he was moved to the intensive care unit. Tests for immune system problems and immune cell levels came back normal. A liver tissue sample showed damaged liver tissue with changes in structure, scarring, and signs of swelling caused by certain white blood cells. The patient was then started on steroid medicines. This helped improve his condition. His liver function and signs of swelling in the body also got better.

The patient was sent home after 40 days in the hospital. He was given steroid medicine with the dose slowly going down over time. On day 47 after leaving the hospital, he had a heart scan using a special X-ray with dye. The results were normal. Eighteen months later, the patient had no symptoms at all.

Skin cancer that spread deeper into the skin, with severe sun damage to the skin

Name: Louise
Age: 16
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), a condition that affects how a person communicates and interacts with others

Hospital Course:
Louise is a 16-year-old girl with autism. Testing showed she thinks and learns at the level of a 13-year-old. Louise grew up in a small country village in Italy with both parents until age nine. Her parents then split up. Her father moved her to Canada. There she went to school and got help from mental health doctors. She also received treatment for a related condition called OCD. OCD causes unwanted repeated thoughts and behaviors.

Over 5 years in Canada, Louise worked with many mental health helpers. She attended school with special changes made to help her learn. Later, a court ordered her to go back to Italy to live with her mother. The court did not find that living with her mother would cause serious harm. However, the mental health doctors disagreed. They believed moving Louise back to Italy could hurt her. The change in her surroundings and less access to mental health care for young people would likely make her symptoms worse.

The mental health doctors also looked into claims that the mother emotionally mistreated Louise. During her time in Italy, Louise was reportedly put down and called hurtful names. The doctors also noted that her OCD could make the move to Italy even harder for her.

The doctors conclude that Louise has a complicated situation because of her condition and history. She needs ongoing medical care and support. The mental health doctors say it is important for Louise to have access to mental health services for young people. She also needs special changes at school to help her learn. These services were available to her in Canada. They should also be available wherever she lives now. The doctors suggest watching her condition closely. They recommend regular visits with medical professionals to check her progress and change her treatment plan if needed.

Hospital Course:
The 67-year-old female patient had a stage 3 hole in the macula, the central part of the eye. She came to the hospital on [redacted] because her left eye vision had gotten worse over the past month. The patient had eye surgery to remove the gel inside the eye and peel a thin layer from the retina. A special dye was used to help the surgeon see better. Gas was put in the eye to help it heal. Eye scans taken four weeks after surgery showed the light-sensing layer was still damaged over a wide area. The patient could see 20/100, which means her vision was still limited. At six weeks, the retina had pulled away from the back of the eye in some areas, but not the central vision area. There were several tears in the retina. She had another eye surgery to fix the detached retina. Laser treatment was used to seal the tears. Gas was again put in the eye. At six months, the patient could see 20/40. Eye scans showed the light-sensing layer was healing in many areas of the macula. There was still some damage under the very center of the macula. By one year, the patient could see 20/25, which is close to normal. Eye scans showed the light-sensing layer in the center of the macula had fully healed.

Stage 3 hole in the macula. Detached retina with several tears, but the central vision area was not affected.

Eye surgery to remove the gel inside the eye. Peeling of a thin layer from the retina using a special dye. Gas placed in the eye to help healing. Laser treatment to seal retina tears.

The patient has gotten much better. Her vision improved to 20/25, which is close to normal. The light-sensing layer in the center of the macula has fully healed.

The patient will need regular check-ups to watch her vision and the health of her retina.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
A 9-year-old boy came to our hospital because he suddenly lost vision in his left eye 10 days earlier. This happened after he rubbed his eye very hard. When doctors checked his eyes, they found problems with both. The right eye had a bulging cornea (the clear front part of the eye) with stretch marks and a small surface scar. The left eye had severe swelling and a bulging cornea in the center. This showed a sudden fluid buildup. The doctors found that both eyes had a condition called keratoconus, where the cornea bulges outward. The left eye also had sudden swelling from fluid leaking into the cornea.

Treatment and Procedures:
The patient had a procedure on his left eye to fix the swelling. The doctor used a small needle to drain fluid from the front part of the eye in a clean, germ-free setting. Then the doctor filled this space with air. After that, the air was replaced with a special gas that filled two-thirds of the space. This gas helps push the cornea back into shape. The patient was given eye drops to prevent infection and reduce swelling. The patient was told to lie flat on his back after the procedure.

Outcome:
The patient has been checked by doctors for 12 months. The corneal swelling has completely gone away. The patient now has a light, cloudy scar on the cornea. With contact lenses, the patient can see 6/9, which is close to normal vision. The pressure inside the eye has stayed normal since the procedure.

Impressions and Plan:
The patient was treated for bulging corneas in both eyes and sudden swelling in the left eye. The special gas procedure was used to fix this. The corneal swelling has completely cleared up. The patient's vision has gotten better with contact lenses. The patient has been sent home and should keep seeing eye doctors for a long time.

Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (a type of blood cancer that affects white blood cells)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with fever and neck pain. She had taken antibiotics for this before. The doctor found several swollen lymph nodes under the left arm. A CT scan showed swollen lymph nodes under the arm and bone damage in the spine. A PET scan showed the cancer had spread to many areas of the bone and bone marrow. A bone marrow test did not show large cancer cells. A small piece of tissue was taken from the lymph nodes under the left arm. The test showed cancer cells had spread throughout the tissue. Special lab tests confirmed the type of cancer. The patient was diagnosed with stage IV cancer that had spread to many parts of the body. The risk level was low to medium based on a standard scoring system.

The patient received radiation treatment for the neck area. She chose not to have regular chemotherapy because of the risk of a past lung infection coming back. She was started on two medicines called CAM and PSL. Her fever got better within a few days. The PSL dose started at 20 mg per day for 2 weeks. Then it was lowered to 15 mg per day for 2 weeks. The long-term dose was 10 mg per day. The patient noticed food tasted a little different. This was likely caused by taking CAM for a long time.

Scans taken 6 months later showed the cancer was gone. The swollen lymph nodes and bone problems had improved. The patient still has no signs of cancer 7 months after starting treatment.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 40-year-old woman who came to our clinic for left back pain that lasted 2 months. The physical exam showed nothing unusual. Blood tests showed slightly high levels of adrenaline and another hormone called renin. A detailed scan of the belly area showed growths on both adrenal glands, which are small organs above the kidneys. Doctors first thought these growths might be adrenal gland cancer. The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland and the left kidney. Tests on the removed tissue showed unusual immune cells. More lab tests found that the patient had a rare type of cancer called NK/T-cell lymphoma, which is linked to a virus called EBV. The patient then had a full body scan to see where the cancer had spread. The scan showed the cancer was in the left adrenal gland area, the right adrenal gland, and under the skin of the left thigh.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was found to have NK/T-cell lymphoma linked to the EBV virus. The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland and left kidney. After surgery, the patient received 7 rounds of cancer-fighting drugs using a treatment plan called GLIDE. The patient also had a transplant using their own stem cells. Two follow-up body scans done within one year showed the cancer was gone. There were no signs of cancer in any of the areas where it had been found before. The patient left the hospital with instructions to come back for check-up visits and ongoing care. This summary gives a full record of the patient's health history, treatment, and expected outcome.

This gene change can affect how the body uses certain vitamins.

Treatment:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted] Ethnicity: Unknown Age: 81 Gender: Male
Date of admission: [redacted] Date of discharge: [redacted]
Length of stay: 40 days
Admitting Diagnosis: Infected pouches in the lower bowel, infected appendix, and a pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital after 4 days of not wanting to eat and belly pain. The patient then fell and lay on the floor for 14 hours. This led to a pocket of infection on the left side of the body. The exam showed signs of belly lining swelling, fast heartbeat, low blood pressure, and fast breathing. These signs pointed to a serious body-wide infection. The patient also had long-term kidney problems and was overweight. A special scan of the belly and pelvis showed infected pouches in the lower bowel. This infection caused a pocket of pus that spread behind the belly organs. The patient also had an infected appendix.

Surgery was needed because the patient was very sick. The patient also had other health problems that made surgery risky. These included heart disease from poor blood flow, an uneven heartbeat, and late-stage kidney disease caused by cysts on the kidneys. The doctors removed part of the lower bowel, closed off the remaining part, and made a new opening in the belly for waste to leave the body. This is called Hartmann's procedure. The doctors also removed the appendix. A small amount of infection fluid was found on the left side of the belly. The area behind the belly organs was not opened during surgery. Tubes were placed to drain fluid from the left side of the belly and the pelvis.

After surgery, the patient was taken off the breathing machine on day 1. The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for 8 days. This was because the patient needed extra oxygen due to a lung infection. The patient then moved to the regular surgery ward. The patient later got a worse body-wide infection. Another scan showed a large pocket of infected fluid behind the belly organs on the left side. Two drain tubes were placed through the skin into this pocket of fluid. Even with infection-fighting medicine given through a vein and draining the fluid, the patient died on day 40 after surgery. The cause of death was the worsening body-wide infection.

Summary of Hospital Course:
The 81-year-old male patient came in with infected pouches in the lower bowel, an infected appendix, and a pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs. These problems led to surgery. During the hospital stay, the patient got a lung infection that needed care in the intensive care unit. Later, the patient got a worse body-wide infection. The patient died on day 40 after surgery.

Discharge Diagnoses:
1. Infected pouches in the lower bowel
2. Infected appendix
3. Pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs

The patient was released to the care of his regular doctor. The patient's family was told to watch for any changes in his health. This includes fever, pain, or discomfort. No other instructions are needed after leaving the hospital.

Patient Name: IA, Mr.
Age: 85
Sex: Male

Hospital Course:
Mr. IA, an 85-year-old male, came to the mental health clinic. He was seeing things that were not there. He saw images of people in front of him. He had been treated for high pressure in his eyes for 7 years. This condition affects both eyes and can damage vision. He had been unable to see for the past 3 years. These strange visions had been happening for about 8 weeks before his visit. The doctor checked his eyes and found damage to the back of both eyes. The light-sensitive area in each eye had dried out and broken down. The nerve that connects the eye to the brain looked pale and showed signs of damage in both eyes. All other body and brain tests were normal for his age.

Treatment and Response:
The patient was told that he did not have a mental illness. He learned a way to make the images go away. He was told to close his eyes and blink over and over. This could make the images disappear for a short time before coming back. His family members learned about this condition called Charles Bonnet Syndrome. They were told not to think of it as a mental illness. At first, the patient came back every 2 weeks. Later, visits were spread out to every 4 weeks and then every 6 weeks. His eyesight did not get better during this time. However, the visions went away after 6 months without any medicine. He was then sent home from care.

Condition at Discharge:
Mr. IA left with a clear understanding of the eye-closing and blinking method used to help him. He was reminded not to think of this as a mental illness. He was told to close his eyes often and blink many times if the visions came back. His family members were happy with the information and advice they received. They agreed to watch and make sure the method was being used and working.

Treatment:

The patient chose to continue the pregnancy after learning about the diagnosis. Surgery was done to repair the split lip and roof of mouth.

Follow-up:

The same gene test was done again using blood after birth. The test showed the same missing piece of genetic material on chromosome 1. This confirmed what was found during pregnancy.

Admission: The patient came to the hospital with two weeks of pain in the side of the back and four days of dark brown urine. During the physical exam, the heart had a normal beat with an extra heart sound heard best on the left side of the chest. The patient had strong pain when the doctor pressed on the left side of the back near the kidney. The doctor also heard crackling sounds in the lower parts of both lungs. First blood tests showed low white blood cell count, low red blood cell count, and low platelet count. The tests also showed high creatinine levels, which means the kidneys were not working well. The urine test was not normal.

Diagnosis: The patient was found to have a blocked blood vessel in the spleen, which damaged part of the spleen. The patient also had a heart valve that formed with two flaps instead of three. This valve had a growth on it caused by an infection. The infection did not show up in blood tests that look for germs. A small tissue sample was taken from the kidney. It showed the immune system was causing swelling and damage in the kidney.

Treatment: The patient took two antibiotics called doxycycline and rifampin for 6 weeks. The patient also had surgery to replace the damaged heart valve. During treatment, the side pain got better. There were fewer red blood cells in the urine. The creatinine levels went down, which means the kidneys were working better.

Prognosis: The patient got better during treatment. However, a blood test for a certain protein linked to the immune system stayed high even after taking antibiotics.

Follow-up: The patient should see a regular doctor for checkups. More tests may be needed.

Patient Information:
Name: [NAME]
Age: 69
Gender: Male

Diagnosis:
Heart attack affecting the front wall of the heart, Heart Failure

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital in September 2017 for heart bypass surgery, repair of two heart valves, and replacement of another heart valve. A special wire was placed in the heart, and the heart device was upgraded to help the heart pump better and correct dangerous heart rhythms. A heart monitoring feature was set up and ready to use starting January 2018.

Progress Notes:
In January 2018, the patient had mild heart failure symptoms and normal fluid levels in the body. Blood tests showed reduced kidney function and high levels of a hormone that shows heart stress. The heart monitor score was 8, which is at the high end of normal. On February 5th, the heart monitor sent an alert because the score went above the warning level of 16. A review of the device data showed the score had slowly risen to 17 over two weeks. The patient was called and said he had no symptoms or signs of fluid buildup. A follow-up phone call was made two weeks later. Even though the heart monitor score rose to 25, the patient still felt fine. However, he admitted to drinking more fluids and eating more salt than advised. The patient was told to cut back on fluids and salt. The heart monitor score stopped rising but did not go down. An office visit was then scheduled.

At the office visit, the patient first said he had no symptoms. But during his exercise program, he had mild trouble breathing. The doctor found swollen neck veins and mild ankle swelling. Blood tests showed worse kidney function and higher levels of the heart stress hormone. The heart monitor score was 22. The patient was slowly building up extra fluid in his body. The dose of his water pill was increased. After this change, the patient could exercise better and finished his exercise program. The heart monitor score also dropped to 0.

Follow-up:
At a follow-up visit in April, the patient had no signs of fluid buildup. Blood tests showed better kidney function and lower levels of the heart stress hormone. The patient is now in stable condition with mild heart failure symptoms. The patient has not needed to go back to the hospital for worsening heart failure.

Impression:
The heart monitor was successfully used as part of the heart failure care plan. The monitor may also help guide changes to medicine for patients at home.

The patient is a 45-year-old man. He came to the hospital with pain in his left side, numbness, and weakness in both legs. During the exam, the patient had weak muscles in both legs. Lab tests of the removed tissue showed a condition called Langerhans cell histiocytosis. This is a rare disease where abnormal cells build up and can damage bones. The patient then had radiation treatment on the T8 through T10 area of the spine. After treatment, the leg weakness and numbness got much better.

The patient has been checked for almost 6 years with no sign of the tumor coming back. Discharge instructions included follow-up visits with the regular doctor. The patient should also get regular scans to make sure the bone tumor does not return.

Overall, the patient received excellent medical care from the healthcare team and responded well to treatment.

Discharge Summary
Patient: 39-year-old male

Medical History:
The patient had a history of hay fever. He reported many episodes of dizziness and patches of hives, with chest tightness that happened either with or shortly after exercise over the previous 3 months. Over time, the episodes had become more frequent and severe and required several treatments to relieve his symptoms. The patient was diagnosed with a condition that causes swelling in the food pipe due to a type of white blood cell. This was confirmed through a small tissue sample.

Hospital Course:
The patient was given several medications to treat his throat and chest tightness with exercise, but they did not completely resolve his symptoms. He later tried to avoid wheat and all food for up to 12 hours before exercise but to no avail.

To manage his condition, the patient chose to start a trial of omalizumab, which was given in doses of 300 mg every 2 weeks. No food restrictions were given during this time. The patient reported major improvement, and he was able to exercise three times a week without any symptoms. He had only one episode of mild hives, but it happened when he had missed one of his omalizumab injections. The patient continued to exercise normally, reporting any symptoms that he had and was followed up monthly.

The patient later experienced episodes of hives, greatly increased chest tightness, and swelling around the eyes after at least 15 minutes of exercise. He ultimately had an episode of a severe allergic reaction with hives, difficulty breathing, and facial swelling and was admitted to the emergency room, where he received several treatments to relieve his symptoms. After this episode, omalizumab was restarted at the same doses and intervals.

Follow-up and Outcome:
The patient continued on omalizumab with no further episodes of severe allergic reactions and no restrictions on his activity level. He is expected to continue being followed up monthly and continue exercising normally.

Patient: 37-year-old African-American female with sickle cell disease (a blood disorder)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the clinic with sudden vision loss in her right eye. During the exam, she could only see hand movements with her right eye. Her left eye had normal 20/20 vision. Her pupils responded normally to light. There was heavy bleeding inside her right eye that blocked the doctor's view of the back of the eye. The patient also had some changes to the nerve and blood vessels at the back of her eye.

Treatment and Management:
The patient had surgery on her right eye to remove the blood and treat the bleeding. The doctor used a small camera and laser during the surgery. Some scar tissue was carefully cut away. Other scar tissue was left alone because it was stuck tightly to important blood vessels.

Follow-up:
At the 1-month follow-up visit, the patient reported sudden painless vision loss in her left eye 2 days before. Her right eye vision had improved to 20/100. Her left eye vision was 20/50. Her pupils still responded normally. The doctor looked at the back of her left eye and saw pale patches near the center. This meant some small blood vessels had become blocked. A scan done a few weeks later showed some leftover scar tissue in her right eye. The scan of her left eye showed damage to the inner layers from the blocked blood vessels.

Recommendations:
The doctor offered a special dye test to confirm what was wrong, but the patient said no. The patient should continue to be checked regularly to make sure her condition is managed well.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient, a 19-year-old [ethnicity] male, was admitted because his kidneys suddenly stopped working well. A small tissue sample from his kidney showed damage to tiny blood vessels. When he arrived, the patient had swelling all over his body, some protein in his urine, and swollen glands throughout his body. The patient had not traveled recently and was not taking any medicines. Blood tests showed the patient had low red blood cells and low cell counts that help with clotting. The patient's kidney function got worse, shown by rising waste products in his blood. The patient was diagnosed with Castleman's disease, a rare illness that affects many parts of the body. The patient also had high levels of a protein that affects blood vessel growth.

Treatment and Management:
The patient received 10 blood filtering treatments to remove harmful substances from his blood. These treatments did not help his low blood cell counts or kidney problems. The patient then started cancer-fighting drugs called Rituximab, Etoposide, Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine, and Prednisone for 6 rounds. Within a week of starting these medicines, the patient's kidneys began working normally again. The patient's fever, belly fluid buildup, and swollen glands began to get better after starting treatment. The care team watched the patient closely during his hospital stay.

Hospital Course:
During the hospital stay, the patient's low red blood cells and clotting cell counts returned to normal. The patient's kidneys started working normally again. Blood tests that measure swelling in the body also returned to normal within the first few weeks. The patient stayed healthy for 2 years without needing any medicine.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient received full information about his illness and treatment choices. The patient was told to see his regular doctor and his specialty doctors for blood, cancer, and kidney care. The patient was told to get regular blood tests and imaging scans to check on his health.

Discharge Medications:
The patient was sent home without any medications.

Castleman's disease, a rare illness affecting many body systems, along with damage to small blood vessels in the kidneys and sudden kidney failure.

The patient was told to see his regular doctor within 1-2 weeks after leaving the hospital.

The patient was in stable condition when she left the hospital.

Bladder cancer, a type called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. This is a cancer of the immune system cells that started in the bladder.

Deceased.

None necessary.

The patient is a 43-year-old woman who never smoked. The patient was admitted after having trouble breathing during activity for six months. The patient had several tests done to find the cause. These tests included a chest X-ray and CT scan of the chest. The patient also had a scope passed into the lungs to collect samples. Brain scans and full body scans were also done. These tests showed advanced small cell lung cancer that had spread. The patient started the first round of cancer-fighting drugs called cisplatin and etoposide. The tumor got much smaller with this treatment. After six rounds, the cancer started growing again. The patient then started a second set of drugs called carboplatin and irinotecan. After two rounds, the patient got a lung infection caused by a blockage. The treatment plan had to change. The cancer was no longer responding to standard treatments. The patient started a third set of drugs called CAV. This included three medicines: Adriamycin, vincristine, and cyclophosphamide. The patient received 11 rounds of this treatment. After the 11th round, the cancer started growing again. This treatment could not continue. The patient then started a fourth set of drugs called ICE. This included ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide. The patient had to stop because of bad side effects. A new plan using ICE without etoposide was started as the fourth treatment. The cancer partly shrank with this treatment. The patient's pain slowly went away during this time. The patient chose to stop further treatment. Eight months after finishing five rounds of carboplatin and ifosfamide, the patient came to the emergency room. The patient had trouble breathing and rib pain. A chest CT scan showed the tumor had grown larger. Comfort care was started with a sixth round of carboplatin and ifosfamide. The patient's symptoms got better. Sadly, the patient died from a lung infection caused by food or liquid going into the lungs. This happened 11 days later. The patient lived for about 27 months after starting cancer treatment.

Patient 3 is a 1-year- and 10-month-old boy. He has Ohtahara syndrome, a rare brain condition that causes seizures. He also has serious delays in his growth and learning.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient started having seizures one day after he was born. These seizures caused his arms and legs to stiffen and stretch out. They happened in groups about 10 times a day, with 2 to 3 seizures in each group. At 1 month old, he started having a different type of seizure with muscle stiffening. A brain wave test showed unusual patterns of activity and pauses. The test also showed seizures that moved from one part of the brain to another. A brain scan came back normal. The patient tried four different seizure medicines, but none of them worked. A fifth medicine called oxcarbazepine helped some, but the brain wave test showed a new problem pattern. Doctors did detailed gene testing and found a rare change in his genes. Because of this, doctors gave him a medicine called phenytoin. The seizures stopped after the dose was raised to 12.5 milligrams for each kilogram of body weight per day. The brain wave test got better and no longer showed the problem pattern.

MEDICATIONS:
The patient takes phenytoin. This medicine worked well to stop his seizures.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will keep seeing his doctors for regular checkups.

Hospital Course Summary:

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a healthy 3.5-year-old boy. The patient was admitted because of weakness and pale skin for five days. Two weeks before coming to the hospital, the patient had loose stools for three days. A physical exam showed yellow skin, pale skin, and an enlarged spleen. Blood tests showed low red blood cell levels. The blood sample also showed unusual red blood cells. The patient was diagnosed with a condition where the body attacks its own red blood cells. This is called warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Hospital Course:
The patient received a blood transfusion. The patient then received a strong steroid medicine through an IV. The patient responded very well to this treatment. The patient took steroid pills for four weeks. The dose was slowly lowered over the next five months. The patient got sick again after catching a cold. The steroid pills were restarted and worked well. When the dose was lowered, the blood counts got worse again. A medicine called azathioprine was started. The blood counts got a little worse. After the parents agreed in writing, a medicine called rituximab was started. The patient received four doses, one each week. Two months later, the patient was doing well. After 12 months, blood tests showed the condition was gone. The patient has been healthy with no return of the illness for three years.

The patient was first told he had a spine infection called tuberculosis by a local doctor. He was given medicine for that illness. But the patient got worse, so he was moved to our hospital. He had pain in his lower back. He also had weakness and numbness in both legs. The patient's thinking and memory were normal. The nerves in his head and face were working fine.

Doctors found that the muscles in both lower legs had gotten smaller. The left side had loose muscle tone. Both legs had weak strength, rated 3 out of 5. Reflexes were missing in both legs. The patient had reduced feeling in parts of his right leg. He could not feel light touch or sharp pokes as well as normal. Feeling was also reduced in the area around his buttocks and upper thighs.

Scans showed a small, clearly shaped growth measuring about 1.5 by 0.6 centimeters. This growth was inside the spinal canal and pressing on the lower end of the spinal cord. The growth was located at the middle-to-lower back area. It had clear edges and different shades on the scan images.

Inside, they found a grayish-white sac with one pocket. This sac was growing in the lower end of the spinal cord. The doctors drained the sac and removed almost all of it. Lab tests showed the sac was a harmless cyst lined with skin cells.

After surgery, the patient slowly got stronger. Leg strength improved to 4 out of 5. Feeling for light touch and sharp pokes came back. One month later, the patient had no nerve problems. He could move around and walk with help.

Date of Admission: [insert date]
Date of Discharge: [insert date]

HISTORY:
The patient came in with headaches, neck pain, and vision problems. An eye exam showed that the patient had lost some vision in both eyes. Both pupils were wide open and not reacting to light. There was also severe swelling of the nerve at the back of both eyes.

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT:
The patient had a brain scan using a special dye. The scan showed signs of long-term high pressure inside the skull. These signs included bending of the eye nerves, widening of fluid spaces around the brain, flattening at the back of the eyes, and an empty space where a gland should be. Another test looking at blood vessels in the brain showed that a growth was pressing on a major vein on the right side of the head. Because this growth was causing high pressure in the brain veins, the doctors decided to remove it with surgery. The surgery was done through a cut behind the right ear. The growth was fully removed, and the vein pressure went down right away. Lab tests showed the growth was a type of bone tumor called an osteoblastoma.

POSTOPERATIVE COURSE:
After surgery, the patient developed an infection in the bone behind the right ear. This infection was treated successfully. The headaches went away quickly. The patient's vision slowly got better over the following weeks. At a 4-week eye checkup, vision was 7 out of 10 in the right eye and 4 out of 10 in the left eye. The swelling at the back of the eyes was completely gone. There was some lasting damage to the left eye nerve. A brain scan 4 months later showed the pressed vein was now normal size. The signs of high pressure in the skull had greatly improved.

DISCHARGE PLAN:
The patient was sent home and told to come back for a follow-up visit. The patient and family were told to contact their doctor if the headaches, neck pain, or vision problems come back.

MEDICATIONS:
None.

FOLLOW-UP:
A hospital visit to check on the patient's condition will be scheduled within the next month.

Admitting Diagnosis: Liver scarring caused by Hepatitis B virus with a blood clot in a major liver vein and confusion caused by liver problems.

Hospital Course:
The patient received a liver transplant from a donor. After surgery, the patient stayed in the intensive care unit for close monitoring. The patient took aspirin and nafamostat mesilate to prevent blood clots. The patient also took prostaglandin E1 to widen the connected blood vessels. Tacrolimus and prednisolone helped prevent the body from rejecting the new liver. Ampicillin/sulbactam, fluconazole, and nystatin helped prevent infections.

On day 6 after surgery, the patient became confused and had trouble moving. The arms had weak movement and the legs had very weak movement. A brain doctor checked the patient. Over the next 6 days, the patient had seizures with unusual chewing movements. Seizure medicine helped control these episodes. A brain scan on day 15 after surgery showed that bleeding in the brain had gotten slightly smaller.

Disposition: The patient left the hospital two weeks later. At that time, the patient could blink and shake the head. A follow-up brain scan three months after the liver transplant showed the brain bleeding had shrunk by half.

Diagnosis at discharge: Liver scarring caused by Hepatitis B virus with a blood clot in a major liver vein, confusion caused by liver problems, and bleeding in the brain.

This same gene change was found in the patient's brothers and mother. This means the condition runs in the family.

Diagnosis:

The patient has CCM, which stands for Cerebral Cavernous Malformation. This is a condition that is passed down in families. It causes small clusters of abnormal blood vessels to form in the brain.

Treatment:

There is no medicine that has been shown to work for CCM. This is especially true when there are many small problem areas. For now, the patient and family members will be treated for their symptoms. This includes keeping blood pressure under control and treating headaches.

Follow-up:

The patient should see the doctor and a genetic counselor on a regular basis. The patient should let them know if anything changes or if new symptoms appear.

Discharge Condition:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

History and Findings:
The patient is a 6-year-old boy who came in because he was losing vision in both eyes quickly over 38 days. The patient had mild trouble seeing at night starting one year before coming to the hospital. The patient's eyesight kept getting worse over time. When the patient arrived at the eye center, the pressure inside his eyes was normal. Doctors found many small bumps on the colored part of both eyes. The nerves at the back of both eyes looked pale, and the blood vessels in the eyes were thin. The middle outer areas of the back of both eyes looked spotted, but there were no dark bone-shaped spots. Other body exams showed no problems.

Diagnostic Tests and Results:
A special dye test of the eyes showed bright and dark spotted areas at the back of the eyes. A scan of the eye layers showed thinning and damage in the outer layer of the back of the eye, but the center vision area was still intact. Tests that measure how the eyes respond to light showed no activity in both eyes. No brain response to light flashes was found either. A brain scan showed several spots where the protective covering of nerves was damaged in the right front and side parts of the brain. Both eye nerves were also larger than normal.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient was found to have a condition that damages the back of the eye and causes vision loss, along with swelling of the eye nerves. The patient was given a medicine to reduce swelling for 14 days, then the dose was slowly lowered. After treatment, the patient's vision with glasses slowly got better. The patient also had a gene test that found a change in a gene called OFD1, which was passed down from family members.

Hospital Course:
The patient got better 3 months later, with improved ability to see light in the center of his vision. Blood tests showed lower levels of certain substances that can cause swelling. The brain's response to light in both eyes became normal. However, the test measuring eye response to light still showed no activity.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient should keep checking his vision and have regular eye exams. The family should think about meeting with a doctor who can explain how this condition runs in families.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]
Patient Name: [Patient's name]
Medical Record Number: [Patient's medical record number]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 43-year-old man with no previous health problems. He came to the hospital with a headache, a drooping left eyelid, and double vision. He had no other brain or nerve problems. Eye doctors and brain doctors examined him. A scan of the head and blood vessels was done to check for a bulge in a brain artery. No bulge was found. More detailed scans of the head and eye area were also normal.

While in the hospital, the patient developed stomach pain that got worse after eating. A sound wave test of the belly showed the bowel wall might be thick. A detailed scan of the belly showed thickening and uneven edges of the small intestine wall. It also showed swollen glands in both groin areas. A scan of the chest was done to check for swollen glands there. It showed a large blockage in the right upper heart chamber. This blockage extended into the large vein leading to the heart. This finding suggested a type of blood cancer.

More tests were done, including a heart sound wave test and a detailed heart scan. These showed a growth inside the heart that matched blood cancer. A sample was taken from a swollen gland. The sample showed signs of a fast-growing blood cancer.

The patient was then moved to a cancer hospital for treatment. Treatment began with a drug plan called CHOP. This included four medicines: cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone. Medicine was also given through a needle in the spine. At first, the patient got better. Later, the patient got worse and passed away.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was found to have Burkitt lymphoma. This is a fast-growing blood cancer. It was found using the chest scan and the gland sample.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was sent to a cancer comfort care center for end-of-life care. The family was told to keep giving the patient's medicines as directed. They were told to stay in contact with the comfort care team. The family was also told to call emergency services if any urgent health problems came up.
